title: Jeremiah 44:15–30
context: The men, whose wives burned incense to other gods, the women, and the people of Pathros answer Jeremiah that they will not listen. They argue that when they offered to the queen of the sky they had plenty, and that since stopping they have suffered; the women add that they acted with their husbands’ knowledge. Jeremiah answers that the offerings were themselves the cause of judgment, and announces that the LORD will give Pharaoh Hophra into his enemies’ hands as a sign. The people’s argument is reported in their own terms and within its historical setting. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about interpreting history in the light of God’s word.

verses.text: Then all the men who knew that their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, even all the people who lived in the land of Egypt, in Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
All the men who knew their wives burned incense to other gods, the women standing by, and the people in Pathros answer Jeremiah. A large assembly responds.

Arminian readers see a community openly choosing its own course.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text notes that the husbands knew of their wives’ practice, so the responsibility is shared.

Reformed readers see communal resistance to God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report the response respectfully as the text gives it.

verses.text: “As for the word that you have spoken to us in the LORD’s name, we will not listen to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
They tell Jeremiah, “As for the word that you have spoken to us in the LORD’s name, we will not listen to you.” The refusal is direct.

Arminian readers see an open, deliberate rejection of the prophetic word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The response is frank, without pretense of obedience, unlike the oath of 42:5–6.

Reformed readers see the human will set against God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of refusing God’s word when it is clearly spoken.

verses.text: But we will certainly perform every word that has gone out of our mouth, to burn incense to the queen of the sky and to pour out drink offerings to her, as we have done, we and our fathers, our kings and our princes, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem; for then we had plenty of food, and were well, and saw no evil.
verses.arminianNotes:
They will keep their vows to burn incense to the queen of the sky as they, their fathers, kings, and princes did in Judah, when they had plenty, were well, and saw no evil. They argue from experience.

Arminian readers take the claim seriously as the people’s reasoning.
verses.reformedNotes:
The practice is also mentioned in 7:18. The people’s argument is that prosperity followed the offerings.

Reformed readers likewise report it without ridicule. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of the sky, and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked all things, and have been consumed by the sword and by the famine.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Since they stopped offering to the queen of the sky, they say, they have lacked everything and been consumed by sword and famine. Their experience seems to confirm their view.

Arminian readers see a sincere, if mistaken, reading of events.
verses.reformedNotes:
The people interpret their suffering as the result of abandoning the queen of the sky; Jeremiah will interpret the same history differently (44:21–23).

Reformed readers see how events can be read in opposite ways. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: The women said, “When we burned incense to the queen of the sky and poured out drink offerings to her, did we make her cakes to worship her, and pour out drink offerings to her, without our husbands?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The women ask whether they made cakes and poured offerings to the queen of the sky without their husbands. They point to shared responsibility.

Arminian readers see the women noting that their husbands approved.
verses.reformedNotes:
The women’s words reflect the household setting of the practice, consistent with 7:18, where families take part together.

Reformed readers see responsibility shared by the whole household. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report the women’s words as the text gives them.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to all the people—to the men and to the women, even to all the people who had given him an answer, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah answers all the people, men and women, who had replied to him. The prophet responds to everyone.

Arminian readers see Jeremiah addressing the whole community without singling out one group for blame.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah’s reply takes up the people’s argument from history directly.

Reformed readers see the prophet answering error with God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about responding to sincere but mistaken reasoning with truth, addressed to all who had spoken.

verses.text: “The incense that you burned in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your princes, and the people of the land, didn’t the LORD remember them, and didn’t it come into his mind?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah asks whether the LORD did not remember the incense they, their fathers, kings, princes, and people burned in Judah. God took notice.

Arminian readers see Jeremiah reinterpreting the same history the people cited.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah argues that the offerings themselves were part of the cause of judgment, not a source of past safety.

Reformed readers see God’s knowledge of all their deeds. Both traditions read this as shared ground about interpreting history in the light of God’s word.

verses.text: Thus the LORD could no longer bear it, because of the evil of your doings and because of the abominations which you have committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation, an astonishment, and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD could no longer bear their evil and abominations, so the land became a desolation and curse, as it is today. Patience ended.

Arminian readers see judgment following long-endured rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse answers the people’s claim in 44:18 by giving a different explanation of their suffering.

Reformed readers see God’s patience giving way to justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the long patience of God and the eventual reality of judgment.

verses.text: Because you have burned incense and because you have sinned against the LORD, and have not obeyed the LORD’s voice, nor walked in his law, nor in his statutes, nor in his testimonies; therefore this evil has happened to you, as it is today.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Because they burned incense, sinned, and did not obey the LORD’s voice, law, statutes, and testimonies, this evil has come on them. The cause is restated.

Arminian readers see consequences flowing from chosen disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse completes Jeremiah’s reinterpretation: disaster came from disobedience, not from ceasing the offerings.

Reformed readers see sin as the root of judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about covenant faithfulness and its absence.

verses.text: Moreover Jeremiah said to all the people, including all the women, “Hear the LORD’s word, all Judah who are in the land of Egypt!
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah addresses all the people, including all the women, calling all Judah in Egypt to hear the LORD’s word. A final oracle begins.

Arminian readers see a renewed call to listen, even after the people’s refusal in verse 16.
verses.reformedNotes:
The explicit mention of the women reflects their prominent part in the preceding exchange.

Reformed readers see God’s word addressed to the whole community. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God continuing to speak even to those who have said they will not listen.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘You and your wives have both spoken with your mouths, and with your hands have fulfilled it, saying, “We will surely perform our vows that we have vowed, to burn incense to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to her.” “ ‘Establish then your vows, and perform your vows.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that they and their wives have spoken and acted to perform their vows to the queen of the sky; then let them keep their vows. The response is ironic.

Arminian readers see God allowing them to follow their chosen path, with its consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words are best read as ironic permission rather than approval.

Reformed readers see God giving people over to their chosen course. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Therefore hear the LORD’s word, all Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: ‘Behold, I have sworn by my great name,’ says the LORD, ‘that my name will no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, “As the Lord GOD lives.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD swears by his great name that his name will no longer be invoked by any man of Judah in Egypt with the oath “As the Lord GOD lives.” A severe word.

Arminian readers see the end of a hollow use of God’s name.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse suggests the community still swore by the LORD while worshiping other gods.

Reformed readers see God refusing to be honored in name alone. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: Behold, I watch over them for evil, and not for good; and all the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt will be consumed by the sword and by the famine, until they are all gone.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD watches over them for evil, not good, and the men of Judah in Egypt will be consumed by sword and famine. The image of watching is reversed.

Arminian readers see judgment answering persistent refusal.
verses.reformedNotes:
The language reverses 24:6, where God sets his eyes on the exiles for good. The contrast is sobering.

Reformed readers see God’s justice against unrepentant idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear the verse soberly.

verses.text: Those who escape the sword will return out of the land of Egypt into the land of Judah few in number. All the remnant of Judah, who have gone into the land of Egypt to live there, will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.
verses.arminianNotes:
A few who escape the sword will return to Judah, and the remnant will know whose word will stand, God’s or theirs. Truth will be tested.

Arminian readers see history vindicating God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question of whose word will stand answers the people’s claim from experience in 44:17–18. A few survivors are again mentioned (44:14).

Reformed readers see God’s word proven true. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘This will be the sign to you,’ says the LORD, ‘that I will punish you in this place, that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for evil.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD gives them a sign that he will punish them in this place, so they may know his words will stand against them. A confirming sign is promised.

Arminian readers see God offering evidence to those still able to heed it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sign is described in the next verse.

Reformed readers see God confirming his word by events. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reliability of God’s word, which the coming sign is meant to demonstrate to the community in Egypt.

verses.text: The LORD says, ‘Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, just as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will give Pharaoh Hophra into the hand of his enemies, as he gave Zedekiah into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand. The sign is announced.

Arminian readers see Egypt’s king shown to be no refuge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah does not narrate the fulfillment, and historical reconstructions of Hophra’s end should be held tentatively. The comparison with Zedekiah recalls Jerusalem’s fall (chapters 39 and 52).

Reformed readers see God ruling over kings. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
